articles.content: Home Trending News IIT Delhi builds India’s first working indigenous micro-GPU for low-cost displays, fishing boats & e-book readers IIT Delhi builds India’s first working indigenous micro-GPU for low-cost displays, fishing boats & e-book readers By developing an indigenous micro-GPU architecture, the IIT Delhi team is working towards a graphics processing solution that could eventually support affordable embedded computing applications. By Devanshu Srivastava 26 Sep 2026 Follow Us New Update A glimpse of the IIT Delhi campus and a micro-GPU IIT Delhi researchers have developed what the institute describes as India’s first working, indigenously designed micro-GPU. The project was developed by M.Tech students Nammi Akash and M. Ravi Teja under the guidance of Prof. Jayadeva and Prof. Kaushik Saha of the Electrical Engineering Department and was demonstrated on a standard Spartan 7 FPGA development board by rendering graphics. The researchers said the development demonstrates the potential of programmable graphics hardware for building affordable computing platforms. According to the researchers, the micro-GPU is designed for devices that require basic graphics and display capabilities. Advertisment Add Startup Pedia As A Trusted Source Unlike large GPUs used in high-end computers, the micro-GPU is designed for applications where a smaller, more affordable graphics processing solution is suitable. What is a Micro-GPU and Where Can it be Used? A micro-GPU ( Graphics Processing Unit ) is a smaller, programmable graphics processor designed to handle graphics-related tasks in embedded systems and other devices. The IIT Delhi team demonstrated its micro-GPU on a Spartan 7 FPGA board, where it rendered graphics. The design has been developed so that it can eventually be implemented on programmable hardware such as FPGAs or incorporated into a chip. The researchers see several possible applications for the technology. These include industrial display systems, simple human-machine interfaces, e-rickshaw dashboard navigators, navigation terminals for small fishing boats, and educational e-book readers. The technology is therefore aimed at everyday and specialised devices that require basic graphics processing rather than high-performance computing or gaming applications. Prof. Jayadeva said the project involved several innovations to implement the design on a standard FPGA board. The work also brings together arithmetic hardware, programmable architectures, compilers, and embedded systems concepts within a single framework. Alongside the hardware development, the researchers are also working on an optimised compiler and software tools that can work with the processor. The team is further exploring a proof of concept using a 65nm chip-making process. It plans to seek funding for chip development, system integration, and eventual commercialisation. The researchers said their objective was to create a compact but genuinely programmable graphics processing architecture suitable for FPGA implementation and future ASIC realisation.
